idiom_name: BackgroundService + PeriodicTimer + TimeProvider (health-check/observability stack for escalation)
implementation_notes: The .NET hosting stack owns the machinery the classic watchman hand-writes: a BackgroundService supplies the monitor loop with a CancellationToken, PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync gives non-overlapping periodic ticks (.NET 6+) and TimeProvider supplies the clock so the check is testable with a fake provider; the arrival path does an Interlocked exchange of clock.GetTimestamp(). What replaces the classic structure is not just the timer but the surrounding contract - the alert is normally published as a health check, counter or observable gauge and the escalation lives in the monitoring stack, so the watchman itself stays a small hosted service. On .NET Framework or pre-.NET 6 targets the same structure is rebuilt on System.Threading.Timer, whose callbacks can overlap and must be re-armed with Change(Timeout.Infinite, Timeout.Infinite) or guarded by a SemaphoreSlim.
pitfalls: System.Threading.Timer callbacks run on thread-pool threads and can overlap (the timer re-fires regardless of the previous callback); guard the alert path with a SemaphoreSlim/Interlocked or move to PeriodicTimer, whose ticks are delivered one at a time.

DateTime.UtcNow and DateTimeOffset.Now are wall-clock and jump with NTP, DST and manual changes; measure silence with Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(), TimeProvider.GetTimestamp() or Environment.TickCount64, which are monotonic.
An undisposed PeriodicTimer or a BackgroundService whose loop ignores CancellationToken keeps running (and paging) across host shutdown and deployment; always dispose the timer and honour the token.

TimeProvider.System is assumed everywhere unless injected: hard-coding DateTimeOffset.UtcNow inside the watchman makes the grace-window logic untestable, which is precisely the part that needs the injected fake clock.
